checks.claim: Van Helmont was a Flemish doctor (physician) and chemist
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'a Flemish chemist, physician, and natural philosopher' (1579-1644); Wikipedia: chemist, physiologist and physician from Brussels.

checks.claim: Recipe: dirty shirt plus wheat grains in a vessel for 21 days
checks.note: Grokipedia: soiled shirt or rags in a container with wheat grains, 21 days; Wikipedia: dirty cloth plus wheat for 21 days; OpenStax: rags and wheat kernels in an open container for 3 weeks. The original has the shirt placed in the opening of a vessel of wheat, so 'pot' is fine.

checks.claim: Key: mice crept in for food and shelter
checks.note: OpenStax: the open container simply gave mice food and shelter; the true explanation.

checks.claim: Wrong: wheat turned into mice as it rotted
checks.note: This is spontaneous generation itself (van Helmont's own claim was that the ferment turned the wheat into mice); false.

checks.claim: Wrong: sweat from the shirt turned wheat into mice
checks.note: Van Helmont's own theory (leaven in the soiled shirt acting on the wheat); false as an explanation.

checks.claim: Wrong: mice formed from warm air in the pot
checks.note: False.

checks.claim: Context: spontaneous generation = life from lifeless matter with no parents; Aristotle taught it about 2000 years before
checks.note: Aristotle (384-322 BC), On the Generation of Animals, ca. 350 BC; van Helmont's recipe early 1600s (Ortus medicinae printed 1648): about 1950-2000 years, 'some two thousand' is fair.

checks.claim: Redi was a doctor at the Medici court in Florence
checks.note: Grokipedia: first physician (archiatra) to Grand Duke Ferdinando II from 1666, at court since at least 1660; Linda Hall: 'a physician at the Medici court in Florence'.

checks.claim: He watched meat, fish and dead snakes rot; flies of the same kinds settled before the maggots; the maggots later became flies
checks.note: Bigelow's English translation: the June snakes in a box, worms turning egg-shaped then flies; fish (barbel) in a box with eggs in bunches; many meats; 'before the meat grew wormy, flies had hovered over it, of the same kind as those that later bred in it'. 'One summer' is a loose but harmless framing (the snake work was in June, the flasks in July).

checks.claim: Key: maggots hatch from eggs flies leave
checks.note: Linda Hall: 'He surmised that perhaps flies laid the eggs that produced the worms.' Redi 1668: 'dal seme delle sole mosche'; Bigelow: derived 'from the droppings of flies, and not from the putrefaction of the meat'.

checks.claim: Wrong: grow from the rot
checks.note: The view Redi was doubting (putrefaction of the meat); false.

checks.claim: Wrong: form from the meat's juices in heat
checks.note: Spontaneous generation; false.

checks.claim: Wrong: come from small worms living inside animals
checks.note: Maggots in carrion are fly larvae; false and not Redi's suspicion.

checks.claim: Context: he found eggs on meat and fish like the clusters flies leave; said only an experiment could settle the doubt; a maggot is a young fly hatched from an egg
checks.note: Bigelow: 'a great many tiny eggs adhering in bunches' on the fish, meat covered 'not alone with worms, but with the eggs'; 'Belief would be vain without the confirmation of experiment'. Grokipedia Maggot: larval stage of flies, from eggs (flesh flies larviposit, but their larvae still hatch from eggs inside the mother).

checks.claim: Snake, river fish, small eels of the Arno, a slice (cut) of veal into four wide-mouthed flasks, in July
checks.note: Redi 1668: 'a mezzo il mese di luglio', 'una serpe, alcuni pesci di fiume, quattro anguillette d'Arno, ed un taglio di vitella di latte', 'fiaschi di bocca larga'. Bigelow: 'four large, wide-mouthed flasks'; Linda Hall gives the same list.

checks.claim: Mouths tied tightly with paper
checks.note: 'serrate benissimo le bocche con carta, e spago, e benissimo sigillate'.

checks.claim: Four more filled the same way and left open
checks.note: 'in altrettanti fiaschi posi altrettante delle suddette cose, e lasciai le bocche aperte'.

checks.claim: He watched them for months
checks.note: 1668 text: no maggot in the sealed flasks 'ancorchè sieno scorsi molti mesi'. Bigelow's translation of the 1688 edition reads 'though many days had passed', but both say the veal dried 'after many weeks' ('dopo molte e molte settimane', djvu/32), so a span of weeks to months is secure and the question cites the 1668 book.

checks.claim: Key: maggots in open flasks, none in sealed
checks.note: 'the sealed flasks produced no worms, while the open flasks bred worms aplenty'; Redi 1668: 'ne fiaschi serrati non ho mai veduto nascer' un baco'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices (reverse, all, none)
checks.note: All false: 'No maggots appeared in the sealed jars'; the open jars bred them.

checks.claim: Context: flies came and went at will; now and then a maggot outside at the lip trying to get in; published 1668 as Experiments on the Generation of Insects
checks.note: Bigelow: 'flies were seen entering and leaving at will'; a maggot on the outside 'that eagerly sought some crevice by which to enter' (1668: 'per di fuora sul soglio', on the rim; Bigelow says on the paper cover - 'lip of a neck' is a fair rendering). Title and year: Grokipedia Francesco_Redi.

checks.claim: Key: the objection was that the seals kept fresh air from the meat
checks.note: Bigelow: the new test because 'the trial had been made with closed vessels into which the air could not penetrate or circulate'; Wikipedia Spontaneous_generation: sealed jars lacked air, so he used gauze.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: dried out, trapped heat, kept off sunlight
checks.note: None is the objection Redi named or answered; the gauze test addressed air. (The drying distractor sits close to the veal's real drying, see the context check; it is still not the objection, but it could be swapped for a cleaner one such as 'The seals had pressed the flies' eggs into the meat'.)

checks.claim: Context: paper and string shut out air as well as flies; next test let air in but kept flies out
checks.note: Correct.

checks.claim: Context: 'The meat had not dried out: the fish in the sealed flasks broke down into a cloudy liquid.'
checks.note: The veal in the sealed flask DID dry out: 'la vitella, dopo molte e molte settimane, rimase arida e secca' (1668); Bigelow: 'after many weeks, became hard and dry'. The fish did turn to a thick turbid fluid and the snake stayed whole. Fix: 'The sealed meat did not simply stay fresh either: the fish broke down into a cloudy liquid and the veal slowly dried hard, yet no maggot appeared in any of them.' (facts.md F10 and M6 also omit the veal.)

checks.claim: Meat and fish in a large vessel covered with very fine gauze, so air could reach it
checks.note: Bigelow: 'a large vase closed only with a fine Naples veil, that allowed the air to enter', set inside a frame covered with the same net; 1668: 'sottilissimo velo di Napoli'.

checks.claim: Flies gathered around it, drawn by the smell
checks.note: Redi says the flies buzzed round the vessel ('ronzare intorno intorno i mosconi') and gives the meat's smell as what drew the maggots ('tirati dall'odor delle carni'). Flies drawn to carrion by smell is plain biology, so the stem is not wrong; writer may prefer 'Flies buzzed around it' to match Redi exactly.

checks.claim: Key: maggots on the gauze, never on the meat
checks.note: OpenStax: 'maggots were also found on the gauze'; Bigelow: 'I never saw any worms in the meat, though many were to be seen moving about on the net-covered frame'; Wikipedia: 'they appeared on the cloth'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: on the meat; on neither; on the meat after weeks
checks.note: All false: never on the meat, and maggots were seen on the net.

checks.claim: Context: flies left maggots on the gauze; a few wriggled into the tiny holes before Redi picked them off
checks.note: 'vi partorivano i bachi'; 'penetravano per i sottilissimi fori del fitto velo'; Bigelow: they 'would have entered the vase had I not speedily removed them'. Correctly says maggots, not eggs, were left on the gauze.

checks.claim: Four sealed flasks with snake, fish, eels, veal; four more with the same meats left open, the covering the only difference
checks.note: 'in altrettanti fiaschi posi altrettante delle suddette cose, e lasciai le bocche aperte'. Redi says 'poscia' (then), i.e. right after; 'at the same time' is a fair simplification of the same set-up, compared over the same period.

checks.claim: Key: the open flasks were a check that the meat could breed maggots
checks.note: Open containers 'soon swarming with maggots'; the comparison that gives the sealed result meaning.

checks.claim: Wrong: spare set; repeat of the sealed test; group where nothing happens
checks.note: All false: the open flasks were not spares, were not sealed, and bred 'worms aplenty'.

checks.claim: Context: many textbooks call the open flasks the control
checks.note: Classroom sources do name the open jar the control; Linda Hall names the sealed flasks the controls. 'Many textbooks' is hedged correctly and the key avoids the word.

checks.claim: Kircher was a famous German priest and scholar
checks.note: 'a German Jesuit priest, scholar, and polymath', born 1602 in Geisa near Fulda; affirmed spontaneous generation in Mundus Subterraneus (1665).

checks.claim: Kircher's recipe: dead flies soaked in honey water, warmed over ashes, tiny worms that grow wings and become flies
checks.note: Redi quotes Kircher's twelfth book of the Mondo sotterraneo: 'acqua melata', a copper plate ('piastra di rame') over warm ashes, worms seen only through the microscope, 'spuntando l'ali dal dorso'. Bigelow: 'besprinkled and soaked with honey-water', 'little by little grow wings'.

checks.claim: Key: Redi wrote the honey water only drew living flies
checks.note: Bigelow: honey-water 'only serves to attract the living flies to breed in the corpses of their comrades'; 1668: 'non serva ad altro che ad invitar più facilmente le viventi'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: revived the flies; turned them into worms; fed hidden worms
checks.note: None is what Redi said the honey water did.

checks.claim: Context: dead flies in a sealed vessel bred nothing; maggots appeared among dead flies in an open one
checks.note: 'nulla nascer mai si vide nel vaso serrato'; in the open vessel maggots appeared and became flies of the same kind. Bigelow: 'I never saw anything breed in the closed vessel'.

checks.claim: After Redi, microscopes revealed tiny organisms in water and infusions, which some took as spontaneous generation
checks.note: Grokipedia: the microscope 'revealed animalcules ... in stagnant water, infusions', read by proponents as spontaneous generation at small scales (Leeuwenhoek, 1670s, after the 1668 book).

checks.claim: Key: his experiments looked only at creatures big enough to see
checks.note: Redi's work dealt with visible insects; microbes reopened the question.

checks.claim: Wrong: proved wrong; too short a time; meat cannot support tiny life
checks.note: All false: Redi's result stands; the sealed flasks ran for weeks to months; microbes thrive on meat and broth.

checks.claim: Context: question stayed open nearly 200 years until Pasteur's flasks in the 1860s
checks.note: Grokipedia: Pasteur's experiments 1861-1864 (Alhumbert Prize offered 1860); 1668 to the early 1860s is about 193 years. Wikipedia dates the key swan-neck experiment to 1859; 'the 1860s' still fits the work that settled it.

checks.claim: Needham was an English priest who worked with microscopes
checks.note: 'English naturalist, microscopist, and Roman Catholic priest' (1713-1781).

checks.claim: He boiled mutton broth briefly in the 1740s and sealed it in flasks; days later it swarmed with tiny life
checks.note: Grokipedia: mutton broth, boiled briefly, corked, 1748, organisms after 'several days to weeks'; Grokipedia Spontaneous_generation and OpenStax: 1745. Either way, the 1740s.

checks.claim: Key: boiling was thought to kill all life in it
checks.note: Wikipedia: 'Believing that boiling would kill all living things'; OpenStax: boiled 'hoping to kill all preexisting microbes'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: longer boiling gave more life; only boiled broth grew life; only mutton broth grew life
checks.note: All false: Needham used many infusions (broth 'infused with plant or animal matter'), unboiled broth also grew life, and Spallanzani's longer boiling gave none.

checks.claim: Context: Needham credited a life force; Spallanzani, an Italian priest, boiled an hour or more, sealed tight, nothing grew; Needham's short boil most likely left tiny life alive
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'an Italian Catholic priest'; boiled 'often up to an hour or more', sealed hermetically by melting the glass, no growth; Needham's 'vegetative force'. Wikipedia (Needham): boiling time 'insufficient to kill any endospores'; OpenStax: he likely did not boil long enough. Contamination through his corks while cooling is the other part of the modern explanation; 'most likely' keeps the line true.

unit_notes: 8 ok, 1 error, 0 uncertain. The one error is in a context: the veal in Redi's sealed flask dried hard over many weeks (1668 text and Bigelow), so 'The meat had not dried out' is false; facts.md F10 and M6 should add the veal. Edition note: the 1668 text says the sealed flasks stayed clear 'molti mesi' (many months); Bigelow's English (from the 1688 edition) says 'many days'. The veal's 'many weeks' backs a long span, so the months wording stands. Redi says the smell drew the maggots, not the flies (cf4c2577aa stem); harmless, but 'Flies buzzed around it' would match him exactly.
